passage:
Monday: Four friends argued about the route for the hostel trip, and Uday sat at the end of the bench peeling the label off a bottle. Deepak noticed, and said nothing yet.
Wednesday: While the others argued, Deepak leaned over. "Uday, what do you think? No pressure, pass is fine too." Uday hesitated. "The night bus loses a whole day. The lake stop is better on the way back." The others paused. "Huh, that's actually smart," said Meghna.
Saturday: Uday sent a short plan to the group chat. Deepak was first to reply: "Booked it the way Uday said." Meghna sent three thumbs up, and Uday sent back a photo of the lake.

qa.q: What was Uday doing at the end of the bench on Monday?
qa.a: Peeling the label off a bottle.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling while sitting at the end of the bench?
qa.a: Left out or unsure about speaking. Uday stayed quiet and fiddled with the label while the others argued.

qa.q: What made Deepak's question easy for Uday to answer?
qa.a: Deepak asked what Uday thought and added "No pressure, pass is fine too," so Uday could say yes or no without being cornered.

qa.q: What is it like for the others when Uday speaks up?
qa.a: They are surprised and interested. They pause, and Meghna says it is actually smart, so the plan improves.

grounding: A young adult asks a quiet friend what they think without pressure, and the group's plan becomes richer.

passage: Kiran, sit. I'm Kavitha, and let me tell you about my second year in the hostel. Five of us prepared for the exam around one table, and the talk belonged to the loud ones. Lata sat with her notebook closed, and I saw her pen tapping. I could have carried on with my own point. Instead I turned and said, "Lata, what do you think? Only if you want to." Lata blinked. Then, slowly, she said the problem we had been stuck on could be solved the other way round. Nobody spoke for a moment. That night the table felt wider. Lata says even now that it was the first time anyone had waited for her.

qa.q: How many people studied around the table?
qa.a: Five, including Kavitha.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when watching Lata's pen tapping?
qa.a: Concerned for Lata, sensing Lata had something to say but was not being given a gap to say it.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make that changed the evening?
qa.a: Kavitha set aside the point Kavitha was making and asked Lata, "What do you think? Only if you want to."

qa.q: How might Lata have felt when the whole table waited for the answer?
qa.a: Heard and valued, maybe a little nervous at first, since Lata blinked before answering slowly.

grounding: An older person recalls asking a quiet member of the study group for a view, opening a turn without pressure.

passage: The café near campus was so loud the study group had to lean in to hear each other, and the project was due in two days. Four of them talked over one another about the marketing plan: Rishi, Anu, Priyam and Preeti. Eshaan, who'd joined the course late, sat with his notebook open, pen still. Preeti noticed he had written half a page. When there was a small gap, she turned to him. "Eshaan, you've been writing a lot. What do you think? No pressure." Eshaan looked up, surprised. "Um. I was thinking we could do a short video instead of a poster. Most students watch reels, not notice boards." The table went quiet. "That's actually brilliant," Anu said. They rebuilt the plan around it in twenty minutes. On the way out, Eshaan said to Preeti, "Thanks for asking." She smiled.

qa.q: What did Eshaan suggest instead of a poster?
qa.a: A short video, because most students watch reels, not notice boards.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when Preeti asked him?
qa.a: He was surprised, then encouraged, sharing an idea he had been sitting on.

qa.q: What made Preeti's way of asking work well?
qa.a: She waited for a gap, pointed to his notes, and added 'no pressure', opening a turn without putting him on the spot.

qa.q: How did the group benefit from hearing Eshaan's idea?
qa.a: They got a better plan, rebuilding around the video in twenty minutes, which made the discussion richer.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a noisy group asking a quiet member what he thinks without pressure, which makes the discussion fairer and richer.

passage: At the drama society meeting in a Jayanagar classroom, the same three voices had been running the discussion about the annual play for forty minutes. Rashmi noticed Chinmay in the corner, nodding, saying nothing, though he had directed two plays in school. When the loudest member paused to check her phone, Rashmi said, "Chinmay, you've directed before. What would you do with the second act?" Chinmay hesitated. "I'd cut the long speech and show it instead. Maybe with shadows." There was a pause. Then the others leaned forward. "Shadows how?" For the next fifteen minutes, Chinmay talked, sketching on the board. The play changed. After the meeting he walked out beside Rashmi. "I didn't know how to get in," he said. "It felt like there was no space." "There was," Rashmi said. "Someone just had to make it."

qa.q: How many plays had Chinmay directed in school?
qa.a: Two plays.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling before Rashmi asked him?
qa.a: He felt shut out and unsure how to join, since it seemed there was no space for him to speak.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that made the meeting fairer?
qa.a: She used a pause to ask Chinmay a specific question based on his experience, opening a turn for him.

qa.q: How did the others respond once Chinmay spoke?
qa.a: They leaned forward, asked questions, and let him sketch his idea, which changed the play.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking a quiet friend what he thinks, opening the floor and making the conversation richer.

passage:
"So Goa or Manali?" said Ravi.
"Goa, obviously," said Tina.
"Manali's cheaper," said Varsha.
"But Goa has beaches!"
They went on for ten minutes. Pradeep noticed Madhuri, curled on the beanbag, hadn't said a word.
"Madhuri, what do you think?" he asked. "You don't have to pick."
Madhuri blinked. "Actually... I was thinking Hampi. It's closer, it's cheaper, and there's the river and the ruins."
"Hampi?" said Ravi.
"My cousin went. She said the sunsets are unreal."
Tina sat up. "Wait, that sounds amazing."
"And no one's fighting about it," Varsha laughed.
Madhuri smiled, a bit shy. "I didn't want to interrupt."
"You weren't interrupting," Pradeep said. "We needed a third idea."

qa.q: What place did Madhuri suggest?
qa.a: Hampi.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhuri felt hesitant to speak?
qa.a: Madhuri said 'I didn't want to interrupt' and smiled shyly after sharing, which shows Madhuri felt unsure about joining in.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep's question work?
qa.a: Pradeep asked directly but added 'You don't have to pick', which opened a turn without pressure.

qa.q: How did the group respond to Madhuri's idea?
qa.a: They loved it, and Varsha laughed that no one was fighting about it anymore.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking a quiet friend her opinion without pressure, which makes the group conversation fairer and richer.

passage: I'm Vikas, and I keep thinking about our group project meeting last month. Five of us around a canteen table, and as usual Rohit and I were doing most of the talking. Neelam had her laptop open and had typed something twice, then deleted it. I noticed because I used to do that in first year. So when Rohit paused, I turned to her. "Neelam, you've looked at the data more than any of us. What do you make of it? No pressure if you're still thinking." She hesitated, then said the survey question on page three was confusing, so half the answers were probably wrong. She was right. We redid it. Looking back, it took one question. Now she speaks up without being asked, and our project got the best marks in the class.

qa.q: What problem did Neelam point out?
qa.a: She said the survey question on page three was confusing, so half the answers were probably wrong.

qa.q: Why did Vikas pay attention to Neelam typing and deleting?
qa.a: Vikas remembered feeling unsure and hesitant like that in first year, so it seemed like a sign Neelam had something to say.

qa.q: What made Vikas's question easy for Neelam to answer?
qa.a: It named her real knowledge of the data and added "no pressure if you're still thinking", so it opened a turn without putting her on the spot.

qa.q: What was it like for Neelam to be asked that way?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous but valued, which helped her share the problem she had been holding back.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a quiet friend holding back in a group and opening a turn for her without pressure.
